title: Setup and Seating
section: The Four Winds Around Your Table
text:
The Four Winds Around Your Table
American Mahjong is played by four players, each representing one of the cardinal wind directions.
East - The dealer and starting position
South - Sits to East’s right
West - Sits across from East
North - Sits to East’s left
Fun Fact: The wind seating doesn’t follow a traditional compass layout. In mahjong, the winds follow Asian cardinal points and have traditional associations with seasons (East/Spring, South/Summer, West/Autumn, North/Winter), which may explain why the arrangement differs from a standard compass.














The wind positions rotate throughout the game, giving each player a turn as the dealer. Don’t worry about memorizing everything now, we’ll cover the significance of these positions as we progress through the lessons.

title: The Card
text:
The American Mahjong card is your guide to winning hands. You can purchase this year’s offical card from the National Mah Jongg League. Each line shows exactly what 14 tiles you need to win, using shorthand symbols and helpful notes.



Basic Structure
Every line on the card represents one complete winning hand. The card is organized into different categories, and each hand shows:

Shorthand notation (the tile abbreviations)
Notes (additional details about requirements)
Point values (how much the hand is worth)
Concealed (whether the hand must be concealed, incidated by a C)




Shorthand
The card uses these standard abbreviations:

1-9: Numbered tiles (any suit: dots, bams, or craks)
D: Dragon
0: Soap (white dragon, can be paired with any suit)
N, E, W, S: Wind tiles (North, East, West, South)
F: Flower tiles



Examples
11 22 333 444 5555
This means you need 2 ones, 2 twos, 3 threes, 3 fours, and 4 fives
FFFF 11 22 333 DDD
This means you need 4 flowers, 2 ones, 2 twos, 3 threes, and 3 dragons



Essential Vocabulary
Understanding these terms is crucial for reading the card:

Pair: 2 identical tiles
Pung: 3 identical tiles

Kong: 4 identical tiles
Quint: 5 identical tiles




Reading the Notes
The notes next to each line give you critical information:
Suit Requirements

“Same suit” = All numbered tiles must be from the same suit
“Any 3 suits” = Use tiles from exactly 3 different suits
“2 suits” = Use tiles from exactly 2 suits

Special Conditions

“X” = The pungs (sets of 3), kongs (sets of 4), or quints (sets of 5) can be called from the discards
“C” = Conceled. NO tiles cannot be called from discards
“Consecutive numbers” = Numbers must be in order (like 1-2-3)



Example
FFFF 11 22 333 DDD (Any 3 Consec. Nos. with Matching Dragons)
This means you do not need exactly 11 22 333, but you can use any 3 consecutive numbers (i.e. 44 55 666 or 77 88 999 would also work!). The dragons must match the suit, (i.e. if you numbers are all bams, you must use the green dragons, if your numbers are all craks you must use the red dragon, if your numbers are all dots you must use the white dragon (soap!)).




Color Coding
When numbered tiles appear in the same color on the card, they must all be from the same suit.
Different colors mean you must have different suits for those tiles.
This visual system helps you quickly identify suit requirements at a glance.


Example
22 44 44 666 8888 (Any 3 Suits)
This means that the suit for the 22 and 44 must match, the suit for the 44 666 must match (and be different from the 22 44 suit), and the 8888 must be in the third suit.



Common Card Sections
The hands are grouped into sections that appear year after year:
{Year}: Hands using the current year with numbered tiles and soaps (e.g. 2025)
2468: Hands with only even numbers
Any Like Numbers: All numbers are the same (e.g., all 3s)
Math Sections: Some cards include multiplication/addition themes (e.g., FF 1111 + 6666 = 7777)
Quints: Hands including 5-of-a-kind groupings
Consecutive Runs: Numbers in increasing order (e.g., 1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
13579: Hands with only odd numbers
Winds and Dragons: Hands featuring mostly winds and dragons
369: Hands using the numbers 3, 6, and 9
Singles and Pairs: Hands with only single tiles and pairs


How to Use the Card

Pick a category that matches tiles you’re collecting
Read the shorthand to see what tiles you need
Check the notes for specific requirements
Count to 14 to verify it’s a complete hand

The combination of shorthand + notes tells you exactly what you need to win!

Pro tip: The notes are just as important as the shorthand - read both carefully. Higher point values usually mean more restrictions, but if you’re playing for a score they’re worth more when you win!

title: The Charleston
text:
After the tiles are dealt, the game begins with a Charleston - a series of tile exchanges between players. Each Charleston consists of three passes, with each player passing exactly 3 tiles during each pass.
The final pass of a Charleston can be a blind pass. Instead of selecting 3 tiles from your hand, you can choose 0, 1, or 2 tiles from your own collection and complete the set of 3 by including tiles you just received from another player (without looking at them first).
If all players agree, you can complete two full Charlestons before starting the main game. The order of the passes are:
First Charleston: Right → Across → Left
Second Charleston: Left → Across → Right
After the Charleston(s), players may make an optional courtesy pass with the player sitting across from them. Both players must agree on how many tiles to exchange (0-3 tiles each). Either player can decline to pass any tiles.
Let’s practice!


Practice the Charleston:
Select 3 tiles to pass each time. Drag the tiles to the correct player.
First Charleston: Right → Across → Left
Second Charleston: Left → Across → Right
Blind passes can be made on the 2nd Left and 2rd Right.
